title: Which Customer, Product, Region or Discount Policy Explains a Falling Contribution Margin?
tagline: Revenue Atlas: a margin bridge that reconciles to a shipment-line ledger to the cent. A pure-Python contract (historical cost, dated FX, freight allocated once per line with a zero residual, credits on returns) verified against a hand-calculated fixture, an independent SQL recomputation on PostgreSQL in GitHub Actions, and the same contract re-implemented in TypeScript for a static demo. Synthetic data; project 01 of the Business Data Lab.
tech: Python 3.11 (decimal domain, no floats on money)
SQL reference recomputation (window functions, largest remainder)
GitHub Actions (postgres:16 service, hosted runners only)
79 Python tests, 166 TypeScript golden checks, 24 browser tests
note: Everything is synthetic: the distributor, its 48 customers, 36 products, 2,400 orders and every figure come from a seeded generator whose designed relationships and injected defects are published in an injection manifest. The public site is a static demo: its calculations run in the browser over a published snapshot, scenario edits live in memory and a reload restores the snapshot. The transactional behaviour (ingest, cost resolution, returns, freight allocation, idempotency, conflicts) is verified separately on GitHub-hosted runners against a transient PostgreSQL, not on the public site. Built from a written specification (Business Data Lab, project 01) by a coordinating session delegating bounded work to implementation subagents; not a measurement of any real business.
problem:
Month-end margin reviews argue from spreadsheets that use different populations: bookings in one, shipments in another, credits netted in the month of the original sale, and order freight joined to line rows so that it is counted once per line. The review cannot say which customer, product, region or discount policy explains a decline, because the totals do not reconcile to anything.

Revenue Atlas fixes the definitions first. Every metric is a sum over shipment lines in a half-open UTC window; every dollar of discount, cost, credit and freight belongs to exactly one line; and the bridge from gross sales to contribution margin must reconcile to the ledger to the cent before anyone draws a conclusion.
built:
Three implementations of one contract, checked against each other and against a hand calculation.

  • The contract (docs/contracts.md): shipment-line grain, shipped-at time basis, half-open windows, dated FX with quarantine for a missing rate, exactly one cost version per line, discounts and freight allocated by largest remainder with a deterministic tie-break, credits on returns at the original cost version.
  • A known-answer fixture written before any code: two shipped lines, net 225, COGS 140, gross profit 85, freight 12 and 3, contribution 70; one returned unit credits 90 and reverses 60, so contribution becomes 40. A standard-library script reproduces it from the source records independently of the application.
  • The Python domain and the FastAPI commands: ingest with raw rows preserved and malformed currencies rejected, cost resolution, partial returns that cannot exceed the remaining quantity, freight allocation guarded by a primary key so a many-to-many join cannot allocate twice; idempotency keys, optimistic versions, 409 and 422 contracts; migrations and an independent SQL recomputation on PostgreSQL.
  • The static site: the same contract in TypeScript on BigInt fixed-point decimals, an executive overview, the margin bridge with drill-through to the transaction ledger, filters in the URL, CSV export with the contract version, dataset hash and filters in its header, and a case study.

steps.title: Write the answer before the code
steps.body: The fixture is the oracle. Its expected values are hand-written literals, and the reference script that recomputes them imports nothing from the application. The Python domain, the SQL recomputation and the TypeScript domain are each tested against that file, never only against each other.

steps.title: Allocate once, reconcile to zero
steps.body: Freight is allocated per shipment over its lines by gross-sales weight: each share is truncated to cents and the leftover cents go to the largest fractional remainders, lowest line id first. The allocation table's primary key is the shipment line, so a second allocation fails with a 409 instead of doubling the cost. The bridge prints the residual; a non-zero residual blocks publication.

steps.title: Quarantine, never zero
steps.body: A line with no exchange rate on its shipment date, or with zero or two cost versions, leaves the population with a reason code and is counted on every screen. It is never valued at zero or at a guessed rate, because a silent zero is how a decline gets explained by the wrong cause.

steps.title: Two modes, disclosed
steps.body: Mode A is the backend run on a GitHub-hosted runner with a transient PostgreSQL: 79 tests including the adversarial cases (double allocation, overlapping cost versions, a return larger than what remains, a reversed credit sign, a cancelled order). Mode B is the public site: the same contract in the browser over a published snapshot. The site says so next to every control that only simulates.

steps.title: Look at it at four widths
steps.body: Playwright walks the journey (direct entry, reload on a nested path, bridge to ledger drill, filter, clear, export) and photographs five routes at 360, 768, 1280 and 1920 px and the bridge at 200 % zoom, asserting no horizontal overflow and no console errors. On the golden dataset the browser bridge shows 250, −25, −90, 135, −80, 55, −15, 40.

Checks. The reference script reproduces the fixture exactly; 79 Python tests pass against PostgreSQL 16 on a GitHub-hosted runner; 166 TypeScript golden checks and 24 Playwright tests pass; the TypeScript pipeline over the full snapshot matches the Python pipeline on every metric, rejected and quarantined record. Evidence: the CI runs and the verification ledger in the source tree.

Known gaps, recorded rather than hidden. Credits are windowed by shipment date while the contract says credit date (defect G-01, test written and marked expected-fail); scenario commands and the six later screens (products, customers, regions, returns, discounts, scenarios) are stubs; the Excel workbook and Power BI package are not yet produced.
